title: Differences between varieties grow into differences between species and genera

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Differences between varieties grow into differences between species and genera

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Through natural selection and divergence of character, the small differences between varieties of a species steadily increase until they equal the larger differences between species of the same genus, or even between genera.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Thus the small differences distinguishing varieties of the same species, will steadily tend to increase till they come to equal the greater differences between species of the same genus, or even of distinct genera.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter IV, “Natural Selection”; section “Summary”. Scope: varieties, species and genera of all organisms

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch04-25: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.57

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Continuity can be examined in selected radiations and speciation continua. The rank-based endpoint is partly conventional and global historical coverage is inadequate.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Use genomic, phenotypic and fossil series spanning population divergence to test whether within-species differences accumulate into the distributions observed among species and genera. Continuity of divergence and documented transitions support the claim; persistent qualitative discontinuities in causal processes would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Most datasets do not observe the same lineage continuously from variety to genus.

Taxonomic ranks are not standardized units of difference.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.46

data adequacy: 0.47

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The pattern that named varieties differ less than species, and species less than genera, is close to how ranks are assigned, so a naive comparison has little power. An independent clock or isolation criterion can break that circle for birds, where morphology and trees are both public. That is a proxy on a restricted taxon, and it still does not show that natural selection, rather than any accumulating process, produced the gaps.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Using a rank criterion that does not itself use the measured traits, such as reproductive isolation or node age, compare morphological distances among populations, species, and genera. Steadily increasing distance with time would support the claim; distances that do not scale from variety to species to genus under that independent ranking would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Cross-taxon measurements of the same traits are rare outside birds and a few model clades.

Species and genera are often delimited by the size of the morphological gaps under test.

Variety is not a current rank and must be proxied by populations or subspecies.
